transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], what brings me in is... I've just been living with this constant mix of guilt, fear, and anger since my friend was killed. It's been a while now, and it just hasn't eased up the way everyone seemed to think it would. I'm just tired of feeling this way all the time.
When exactly did your friend pass away? I want to understand how long ago this happened.
Well, it was about two years and three months ago now. We were on a walking tour when she was killed. And... yeah, this has all just been going on ever since then.

When you experience these feelings of guilt, fear, and anger, do you find yourself having unwanted memories or flashbacks of the moment your friend was killed, or is it more of a constant emotional pain about losing her?

It's definitely not just the emotional pain. I do get those unwanted memories. 

Little things will trigger it out of nowhere... like hearing a crosswalk signal, or the loud growl of a truck. Even just seeing a walking-tour map can suddenly put the whole scene right back in my head. It happens so sharply. I can just... see my friend stepping off the curb again before I can even stop it. So, yes, the memories definitely intrude on me.

When you encounter those triggers like the crosswalk signal or the walking-tour map, are you primarily trying to avoid having the flashback of the accident itself, or are you avoiding things because they remind you of your friend and the fact that she's gone?

I'm definitely trying to avoid the memories of the accident itself. It's not about avoiding my friend... it's about avoiding what happened. Like, I go out of my way to avoid that specific intersection completely. I won't drive or walk near it. And I've actually stopped signing up for most tours, or even community safety meetings, because I just cannot bear it when the conversations circle back to what happened there. I just don't want to be reminded of the event.

Besides the flashbacks and avoidance you've described, have you noticed that you feel emotionally numb or detached from things—like difficulty feeling joy or connection to others—or do you find yourself more on edge, jumpy, or easily startled by sudden noises or movements?

Well, it's more of the numbness, I think. I just don't feel much of anything for the things I used to love. 

I used to spend a lot of time planning my garden beds, I'd quilt with the ladies, go to theater outings, and... well, I used to argue happily at my book club. But now, I just look at those things written on the calendar and I feel almost nothing. It's just like... like they belong to someone I used to be. I just don't have it in me to care about them right now.
Since the accident two years ago, have you found yourself blaming yourself for what happened to your friend—like thinking you should have done something differently or that it was somehow your fault?

Yes, I do. I keep telling myself that if I had just picked a different route for us to walk that day, or... or if I had pushed harder about that crossing, she might still be alive. It's hard not to think about what I should have done differently. And then, on top of that, I just get furious all over again at the driver, and at the town for letting it happen in the first place. So, yes, I do blame myself a lot.

Since the accident, have you noticed that your view of yourself or the world has changed in a negative way—like feeling that you're a bad person, or that the world is fundamentally unsafe, or that you can't trust people anymore?

I haven't really noticed feeling like that. I don't think I'm a bad person, and I don't walk around thinking the whole world is completely unsafe or that I can't trust anybody. It's mostly just... well, what I already mentioned, the guilt about that specific day and being angry at the driver and the town. But my overall view of everything hasn't changed like that.
Did these symptoms—the flashbacks, the avoidance, the numbness, the guilt and anger—start right after the accident happened, or did they develop gradually over time, or even start later?
They started pretty much right away. This has all been going on since my friend was killed on that walking tour... so, about two years and three months ago now.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), chronic presentation. She experienced a qualifying traumatic event (witnessing friend's death in traffic accident), with onset of symptoms immediately following the trauma. She demonstrates the core symptom clusters: intrusive memories/flashbacks triggered by reminders (crosswalk signals, truck sounds, tour maps), active avoidance of trauma-related cues (avoiding the intersection, community safety meetings), emotional numbing (anhedonia regarding previously enjoyed activities like gardening, quilting, theater, book club), and persistent negative emotional states (guilt, anger, fear). Symptoms have persisted for 27 months (well beyond the 3-month threshold for chronic PTSD). Functional impairment is evident in withdrawal from valued social and recreational activities. The presentation does not meet criteria for Complex PTSD (F43.12) as there is no evidence of prolonged/repeated trauma or additional disturbances in self-organization. Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) is less likely given the clear trauma-specific triggers and intrusive trauma memories rather than generalized worry.
